attempts.response: {"title":"SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model","authors":"Jaspreet Singh, Thomas Litfin, Jaswinder Singh, Kuldip Paliwal, Yaoqi Zhou","field_subfield":"Bioinformatics / Computational Structural Biology","type_of_paper":"Primary research: new method (protein contact-map prediction)","executive_summary":"This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map predictor that improves single-sequence-based prediction by incorporating attention-map features from the pre-trained transformer language model ESM-1b, alongside one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs, trained with an ensemble of ResNet architectures. The motivation is that most contact-map predictors rely on multiple-sequence-alignment (MSA) and evolutionary-profile information, which is unavailable for many proteins lacking homologous sequences, and generating such profiles is computationally intensive. The authors therefore seek a method that predicts contact maps without homologous information, addressing the limitation of the prior single-sequence method SSCpred, which performs adequately for proteins with few homologs but poorly for those with more effective homologs. The central hypothesis is that unsupervised deep-learning features from ESM-1b, concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs, will outperform both the single-sequence baseline and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs (Neff), and that an ensemble of models trained with different feature combinations will further improve performance. The method was evaluated on three independent test sets: SPOT-2018 (669 proteins), Neff1-2018 (46 proteins with Neff=1), and CASP14-FM (15 free-modeling targets). Results show a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and improvements of 48.7% and 48.5% over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact respectively on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 set. The method is also substantially faster than evolutionary-profile-based methods, making it suitable for large-scale prediction. The study uses a benchmark dataset from ProteinNet (50914 proteins before 2016, clustered at 95% sequence identity), reduced to 39120 proteins after homology filtering, then to 34691 training and 88 validation proteins after length filtering. The architecture uses a 12-block ResNet (the maximum depth trainable on the available GPU), with convolutional layers of channel size 64 and kernel size 3, trained with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.001), batch size 1, and early stopping of 3. Six models were trained with different feature combinations, predicting either inter-residue contacts as binary classification or inter-residue distances as distance bins. The ensemble (SPOT-Contact-Single) outperformed all individual models, with a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model on the validation set. On the Neff1-2018 example protein (5YKZ_A), SPOT-Contact-Single achieved an F1-score of 0.388, compared to 0.215 for SPOT-Contact, 0.235 for TrRosetta, and 0.252 for ESM-1b. The authors note that using ESM-1b attention maps limits direct contact-map prediction to proteins with fewer than 1024 amino acids, but argue this is acceptable since proteins are usually composed of domains with fewer than 1000 residues. In terms of computational efficiency, SPOT-Contact-Single made predictions in 116 seconds on CPU for the CASP14-FM dataset, 22 times faster than TrRosetta, and TrRosetta took 1926 seconds on GPU, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single. The authors acknowledge that profile-based predictors improve over SPOT-1D-Single as Neff increases, indicating that multiple-sequence alignment of homologous sequences can provide co-mutation information more effectively than unsupervised learning. The paper also notes that further improvement may come from using more advanced architectural models such as Transformer or Performer. The study contributes a fast, reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods for large-scale protein contact-map prediction, particularly for proteins without homologs. While the paper does not provide a bibliography in the supplied text, the introduction references numerous prior works, including ESM-1b (Rao et al., 2020), SPOT-Contact (Hanson et al., 2018), TrRosetta (Wu et al., 2020), SSCpred (Chen et al., 2020), and the ResNet architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). The paper's findings are supported by quantitative results across multiple test sets and feature combinations, and the method's design is grounded in prior work on protein contact-map prediction and transformer language models. The study's limitations include the reliance on ESM-1b attention maps, which constrain the method's applicability to proteins with fewer than 1024 amino acids, and the potential for overfitting, mitigated by early stopping and homology filtering. The paper's contribution is significant for the field of protein structure prediction, as it provides a method that can predict contact maps without relying on evolutionary information, which is essential for accurate protein structure and function prediction. The method's speed and accuracy make it suitable for large-scale prediction, which is important for understanding protein structure and function. The paper's findings are consistent with prior work on the use of transformer language models for protein contact-map prediction, and the method's design is grounded in the success of the ResNet architecture in protein contact-map and RNA secondary structure prediction. The study's results are reproducible, as the authors provide detailed descriptions of the method, datasets, and evaluation metrics. The motivation is that most contact-map predictors rely on multiple-sequence-alignment (MSA) and evolutionary-profile information, which is unavailable for many proteins lacking homologs and is computationally expensive to generate. The authors address this gap by feeding ESM-1b attention maps alongside one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs into an ensemble of ResNet architectures. The central hypothesis is that unsupervised language-model features concatenated with existing single-sequence features will outperform both the single-sequence baseline SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs (Neff). The method was evaluated on three independent test sets: CASP14-FM (15 free-modeling targets), SPOT-2018 (669 proteins), and Neff1-2018 (46 proteins with Neff=1). Results show a 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvements over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact respectively on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. The method is also substantially faster than evolutionary methods. The study concludes that SPOT-Contact-Single is a reasonably accurate, fast alternative to evolution-based methods for large-scale prediction, though it cannot directly handle proteins longer than 1024 amino acids due to ESM-1b's input constraint. The strongest evidence is the 45% higher F1-score (0.32 vs 0.22) versus profile-based methods on proteins without homologs, and the example protein 5YKZ_A showing F1 of 0.388 versus 0.215, 0.235, 0.252 for SPOT-Contact, TrRosetta, and ESM-1b. Executive Summary
This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map predictor that improves single-sequence-based prediction by incorporating attention maps from the pre-trained transformer language model ESM-1b. The motivation is that most contact-map predictors rely on multiple-sequence-alignment and evolutionary information, which is unavailable for many proteins lacking homologs, and generating such profiles is computationally intensive. The authors address this gap by feeding ESM-1b's attention maps together with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs into an ensemble of ResNet architectures trained on a large dataset of nearly 35,000 proteins. The central hypothesis is that unsupervised language-model features concatenated with existing single-sequence features will outperform both the single-sequence baseline SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs (Neff). The method was evaluated on three independent test sets: SPOT-2018, Neff1-2018, and CASP14-FM. Key results include a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and 48.7% and 48.5% improvements over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact respectively on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. Feature importance analysis showed that ESM-1b attention maps yield the largest gains, with the last-layer attention maps producing F1, MCC, precision, and AUC of 0.51, 0.50, 0.56, and 0.95. The ensemble of six models improved over the second-best individual model by 4% in F1-score. The method is notably faster than evolutionary methods, requiring 116 seconds versus 2556 seconds for TrRosetta on CASP14-FM. The authors note a limitation that ESM-1b attention maps cannot be used for proteins longer than 1024 amino acids, though this is mitigated by the domain structure of most proteins. The work positions SPOT-Contact-Single as a reasonably accurate, fast screening tool for large-scale contact-map prediction without evolutionary information.

Research Context
The past two decades have seen many developments in the field of protein structure prediction. Improvements in contact-map prediction have contributed to advances in tertiary structure prediction. Most contact-map predictors rely on evolutionary information that is unavailable for many proteins. The reliance on homologs limits performance for proteins lacking homologous sequences. Single-sequence-based methods provide less information for the neural network to learn. Recent unsupervised deep learning methods extract features inspired by NLP language models. ESM-1b is a Transformer-based method that outputs embeddings and attention maps. The gap is the lack of methods that predict contact maps without using homologous information. There is a need to explore features beyond one-hot encoding for single-sequence-based methods. The hypothesis is that unsupervised learning features improve single-sequence-based prediction. The predicted method should outperform SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low Neff. An ensemble of models trained through different approaches should add to the improvement.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether ESM-1b attention maps improve single-sequence-based contact-map prediction. The hypothesis is that language-model features concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs outperform baselines. The predicted outcome is outperformance of SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low Neff. The authors hypothesize that an ensemble of models trained through different approaches adds to the improvement. The method should provide a faster and reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods. The hypothesis is that ESM-1b attention maps significantly boost performance over one-hot encoding. The authors predict that concatenating all features together further increases the F1-score. The hypothesis is that direct contact-map prediction performs slightly better than distance-based prediction. The predicted outcome is that the ensemble outperforms all individual models. The hypothesis is that SPOT-Contact-Single is 45% higher in F1-score than SPOT-Contact and TrRosetta on proteins without homologs. The authors predict that the method is suitable for genomic scale prediction due to speed. The hypothesis is that the method can be used as a reasonably accurate screening tool.

Methodological Details
The study utilized the benchmark dataset prepared by ProteinNet. The dataset consists of 50914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with high resolution. Proteins were clustered at a sequence identity cut-off of 95% according to MMseqs2 tool. The training dataset was chosen with a sequence identity cut-off of 95% to obtain as much data as possible. 100 proteins were separated from the ProteinNet set for validation. Proteins with hits at an e-value cut-off of less than 0.1 were removed. The final training set contained 34691 proteins. Proteins with a length more than 500 were removed from both sets. The final validation set contained 88 proteins. The test set SPOT-2018 contained 669 proteins. The Neff1-2018 test set contained 46 proteins with Neff=1. The Neff1-2018 test set provides a reliable, stringent and completely independent benchmark.

Procedures And Architectures
The input features included one-hot encoding of amino acids, SPOT-1D-Single output, and ESM-1b attention maps. One-dimensional features were converted into two-dimensional features using an outer concatenation. The model used the probabilities of three-state-secondary-structure and eight-state-secondary structure. The features included Solvent Accessible Surface Area, Half-Sphere-Exposure, and backbone torsion angles. Attention maps were gathered using all twenty attention heads from the last layer of the transformer. Attention maps were also gathered from twenty attention heads from every layer of the ESM-1b model. The attention maps were symmetrized and had average product corrections applied. The neural network architecture was inspired by the success of the ResNet architecture. The study used a 12 block ResNet, which is the maximum depth that could be trained on the available GPU. The study employed a recently published version of ResNet that performs better than vanilla and pre-act ResNet. The convolutional layers used a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. The study trained six models with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations.

Key Results
The method made a significant improvement over SSCpred with 15% improvement in the F1-score for the independent CASP14-FM test set. The method outperformed TrRosetta with 48.7% improvement in the F1-score on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. The method outperformed SPOT-Contact with 48.5% improvement in the F1-score on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. The model trained on one-hot encoding of the fasta sequence only predicted the contact-map with an F1-score of 0.15. Adding SPOT-1D-Single output to one-hot encoding improved the F1-score by 22.90%. The attention maps from the last layer of ESM-1b led to 0.51, 0.50, 0.56, and 0.95 for F1, MCC, precision and AUC of ROC. The last-layer attention maps showed 242% improvement in the F1-score over models trained on one-hot encoding. The last-layer attention maps showed 178% improvement in the F1-score over models trained on SPOT-1D-Single + one-hot encoding. The attention maps from all layers showed continued improvement in the precision of all short-, medium-, and long-range contacts. Concatenating all features together showed an increase of 2.92% in F1-score over using the attention maps (all layers) only. The ensemble improved over the second-best individual model by 4% for the F1-score. The performance gain was consistent across all matrices.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The interpretation is that unsupervised learning features provide valuable information for contact-map prediction. The mechanism is that ESM-1b attention maps capture sequence context that improves prediction. The interpretation is that ESM-1b attention maps significantly boost performance over one-hot encoding. The mechanism is that attention maps from all layers provide continued improvement in precision. The interpretation is that the ensemble of models adds to the improvement. The mechanism is that the ensemble takes the mean of individual models to gain improvement. The interpretation is that the method is a reasonably accurate screening tool for protein contact map prediction. The mechanism is that the method does not employ evolutionary information, making it fair to compare on proteins without homologs. The interpretation is that the method is more suitable for genomic scale prediction due to speed. The mechanism is that the method is 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU for CASP14-FM dataset. The interpretation is that the method provides a much faster and reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods. The mechanism is that the method is useful for large-scale prediction.

Contradictions And Limitations
The limitation is that ESM-1b attention maps make it not possible to directly predict contact maps for proteins with more than 1024 amino acids. The limitation is that SPOT-1D-Single is not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods as Neff increases. The mechanism is that multiple sequence alignment of homologous sequence can provide co-mutation information more effectively than unsupervised learning. The limitation is that the method cannot be used for proteins with more than 1024 amino acids. The mitigation is that proteins are usually made of domains with less than 1000 residues. The limitation is that the method is not as competitive as evolution-based methods for proteins with more homologs. The mechanism is that the performance of the profile-based predictors improves over SPOT-1D-Single as Neff increases. The mechanism is that the method is limited by the length of the protein sequence. The mechanism is that the method is limited by the lack of evolutionary information.

Data And Code Availability
The study utilized the benchmark dataset prepared by ProteinNet. The study downloaded all protein structures released between May 2018 and April 2020. The study utilized the web-server available online from http://csbio.njust.edu.cn/bioinf/sscpred/ for SSCpred. The study utilized the stand-alone programs available online from https://github.com/gjoni/trRosetta for TrRosetta. Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study trained a ResNet12 architecture on different input features and compared their performance on the validation set. The study trained six models with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations. The study trained the direct contact-map prediction models using Binary Cross-Entropy loss. The study trained the distogram-based prediction models using Cross-Entropy loss. The study used the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 1. The study trained all models with early stopping of 3. The study examined two different training strategies: direct contact-map prediction and distogram-based contact-map prediction. The study trained different model architectures using a combination of one-hot encoding, SPOT-1D-Single and ESM-1b attention maps (all layers). Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the development of SPOT-Contact-Single, a single-sequence-based contact-map predictor using ESM-1b attention maps. The strongest evidence is the 15% improvement in the F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM and 48.7% and 48.5% improvements over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. The future path is to use more advanced architectural models such as Transformer or Performer for further improvement in protein contact-map prediction without evolutionary information.
